common_name: Rockspray Cotoneaster (Low Spreading Fishbone-Branched Groundcover with Red Berries)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Rockspray tolerates poor, rocky, or dry soil and is often used to stabilize slopes and banks where its low, spreading branches root lightly as they spread.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; established plants tolerate drought, poor rocky soil, and wind, making this a reliable choice for slopes, banks, and low-maintenance beds where little else thrives. Rockspray cotoneaster is named for its distinctive herringbone or 'fishbone' branching pattern, with stiff horizontal branches that hug the ground and layer over each other as the plant spreads, studded with small glossy dark green leaves that turn red-orange in fall. Small white to pink flowers appear in late spring and are followed by abundant bright red berries that persist into winter, providing food for birds and strong seasonal color over bare or rocky ground. It needs minimal pruning beyond removing dead wood, and its low, wide-spreading habit make it a classic choice for cascading over walls and covering banks where mowing is impractical.

common_name: Barbecue Rosemary (Stiff Upright-Stemmed Culinary Rosemary Grown for Skewers)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings after the last frost in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Barbecue's extra-stiff, straight stems are grown specifically to be cut, stripped of leaves, and used as fragrant skewers for grilling.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, slightly alkaline soil, and avoid overwatering since rosemary is far more likely to fail from soggy roots than from drought. Barbecue is an upright culinary rosemary selected for unusually long, straight, rigid stems that hold together well enough to thread meat and vegetables directly onto for grilling, imparting a subtle piney rosemary flavor as the skewer chars. Its needle-like leaves have the same robust, resinous culinary flavor as other upright rosemary types and are equally good stripped fresh for roasting and seasoning. Established plants are drought-tolerant and long-lived in the Gulf South once past their first season, though in zones below 8 they should be grown as a container plant and brought in over winter, since rosemary's hardiness varies considerably by selection.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Herb Gardening

common_name: White Sprouting Broccoli (Hardy English Heirloom Overwintering Broccoli)

planting.note: Start seed in mid- to late summer and transplant in early fall so plants are well established but not yet flowering before winter; the plants overwinter as compact rosettes and send up their edible flowering shoots in late winter to early spring, well ahead of purple sprouting types.

directions: Transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in late summer or early fall, spacing plants wide to accommodate a full season of growth before the harvest of edible flower shoots the following late winter. White Sprouting is a classic English heirloom broccoli grown as a hardy biennial: plants spend fall and winter building a large rosette of foliage, then in late winter to early spring send up a profusion of small, tender, cream-white flowering shoots that are harvested continually over several weeks, much like purple sprouting broccoli but ivory-headed and typically a touch earlier. Regular picking of the central and side shoots before flowers open encourages continued production, and the long harvest window makes it valuable for filling the late-winter garden gap when little else is producing. It needs a long, cool growing season to perform well and is best suited to mild-winter climates like the Gulf South where it can overwinter in the open ground without protection.

common_name: Hayman Sweet Potato (Old-Time Southern Heirloom White-Fleshed Sweet Potato)

planting.note: Plant rooted slips 3–4 weeks after the last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F; Hayman is a long-season Southern heirloom that rewards the full length of a Gulf South growing season with heavy yields of long-storing roots.

directions: Plant rooted slips 4–6 inches deep in loose, well-drained, sandy-loam soil in full sun, ridging the row to keep the developing roots from sitting in wet soil. Hayman is an old-time Southern heirloom sweet potato, once one of the most widely grown varieties across the Carolinas and Georgia before modern commercial types like Beauregard displaced it, valued for its pale tan skin, dry, mealy, cream-white to pale-yellow flesh, and a mild, chestnut-like sweetness quite different from the moist orange-fleshed types now common in supermarkets. Vines are vigorous and heat-tolerant, sprawling widely and shading out weeds once established, and the roots store exceptionally well through winter when cured properly. Cure freshly dug roots at warm temperature and high humidity for about a week before storing to heal skins and convert starches to sugar, improving both flavor and keeping quality.
